newsitem.title: FRANCE: EP opens fire on rules to cut vehicle pollution.
newsitem.headline: EP opens fire on rules to cut vehicle pollution.

text.p: The European Parliament ratcheted up on Thursday draft EU rules on vehicle engine emissions and fuel quality intended to slash air pollution by the year 2010.

The EU assembly adopted dozens of amendments tightening fuel norms and engine standards put forward by the European Commission, criticising the EU executive for having failed to consult more widely than the car and oil industries in drawing up its plans.

In return, the Commission warned it would retain few of parliament's amendments when revising the proposal, saying they were unlikely to win support among EU environment ministers and might even block progress.
The oil industry slammed parliament's stance, saying it ignored three years of research and for fuels, would cost an extra 50 billion European currency units ($57 billion) to meet.
Environmental groups meanwhile attacked parliament's proposed four-year opt-outs for southern European states, which they said would suffer worse air problems than they had now.

French Green Noel Mamere, who wrote the report on fuel quality norms, secured a series of changes to Commission proposals which would allow national capitals to use different tax rates to promote cleaner fuels and requiring two grades of diesel to be made available from 2000, with the dirtier grade being phased out in 2005.

His suggested changes would also cut allowed benzene levels in petrol to one percent from the Commission's proposed two percent for the year 2000 and sulphur content to 30 parts per million (ppm) from 200 ppm. Both substances cause air-borne pollutants which damage human health.
German Socialist Bernd Lange, reporting on vehicle emission standards, won backing for mandatory standards in both 2000 and 2005, not just for 2000 as proposed.

Other changes adopted would provide for national authorities to test different cars' pollution performance and to mandate call-backs of entire fleets for those failing, a system currently operated by Sweden.

Parliament's amendments would also require cold-start tests in new-model approval procedures, bringing in one of the vehicle running conditions which produces some of the worst air pollution in north European winters.

Parliament's amendments go far further than the consensus likely to emerge from a June meeting of environment ministers, one senior Commission official told Reuters ahead of the vote but in anticipation of the outcome.
"Several of the amendments coming from parliament we can accept but we are sticking to our broad proposal," said the official, who declined to be identified.

"We do recognise that parliament is going in the right direction as far as the environment is concerned but we have had major negotiations with industry and we do not feel that we can move away from our proposal too early.
"At the same time, we have to be very careful, if we go too far we might end up in a situation where the Council is blocked, unable to get a common position.
Thursday's vote now leaves the field to the the Dutch, who hold the EU presidency and have pledged to secure initial agreement among ministers at the June meeting.
